Today they see that community put Percy to the test through training, and they study how a hero in training is shaped by it.","enduringUnderstanding":"Heroes in myths are shaped over time through trials, relationships and the values their communities expect of them. Authors arrange episodes in a sequence to show that change.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 15 students read pp. 117–126 and review pronoun case in writing. The homework excerpt from Popol Vuh sets up later cross-text comparison of hero stories from different cultures.","performanceTask":"For Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students must describe how a sequence of events shows character growth. Today they practice by tracing Percy's training episodes and explaining what each one adds."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"pulverize","definition":"to crush into powder; to defeat completely","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"excelled","definition":"did extremely well at something; was better than others","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"technique","definition":"a particular way of doing something that takes skill","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"appraised","definition":"looked at carefully to judge the value or quality of someone or something","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"fates","definition":"the things that will happen to a person in life, as if decided in advance; destinies","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"mortals","definition":"human beings, who will eventually die (in myths, as opposed to gods)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"escort","definition":"to go with someone to guide or protect them","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"hoard","definition":"a hidden store of valuable things that is saved up; to collect and keep a large amount","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"sacrificed","definition":"gave up something valuable, or offered it to a god","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"demigod","definition":"a person who is part god and part human","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"episode","definition":"one separate event or scene in a longer story","tier":"support"},{"word":"sequence","definition":"the order in which events happen","tier":"support"},{"word":"syllable","definition":"a word part with one vowel sound","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 107–116 (Chapter 8)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate what they know about training and how people change through practice, and connect it to Percy's time at camp.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Turn and Talk: Getting Better","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.3"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn to your partner. Think of a time you learned something hard, such as a sport, an instrument or a game. Describe one struggle and one success you had along the way."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What changed in you between your first try and your later tries? Was it only skill, or something else too?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When I learned to swim, I was scared of the deep end and kept quitting. After my coach practiced with me every week, I got better, and I also felt braver. It wasn't only skill. I changed inside too."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Percy is in training too. In Chapter 8, the author gives us a series of training scenes. Today we will track how each one changes Percy and what the camp expects of its heroes."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Take two or three shares, then move to the Literacy Lab. Ask students to bring their copy of the book open to p. 107."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students decode and determine the meanings of Chapter 8 vocabulary using syllabication, word parts and context clues.","activities":[{"id":"lab-syllabication","title":"Break It Down: Syllables in Long Words","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.4"],"routine":"Introduce New Words Using Morphology","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Say each word with your teacher. Clap the syllables, then draw slashes to divide the word: pul/ver/ize, de/mi/god, sac/ri/ficed, ap/praised."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When a word is long, we can split it into syllables, and each syllable has one vowel sound. Look for vowel sounds first. Then look for a consonant between two vowels. Words like *demigod* are also compound-like: *demi-* means half and *god* is a word we know."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How many syllables do you hear in *pulverize*? Where would you split it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Three syllables: pul-ver-ize. I hear a vowel sound in each part. The *-ize* ending makes a long i sound, like in *realize*."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do you notice about *excelled*, *technique* and *escort*? Which have silent or tricky parts?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In *technique*, the *-que* sounds like a k, so it's tech-nique with two syllables. *Excelled* is ex-celled, and the double *l* just makes the *l* sound one time. *Escort* is es-cort with the stress on the first part."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Do not rush to definitions here. The aim is accurate decoding. Have students whisper-read each word twice. Write *hoard* beside *horde* to show a homophone; *hoard* is one syllable."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: dividing words into syllables","tryThis":"Have students tap a finger for each vowel sound they hear while saying the word, then draw slashes between the taps. Start with two-syllable words (*escort*, *technique*) before three-syllable words."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: syllabication","tryThis":"Have students find two more multisyllabic words in pp. 107–116, divide them, and predict meanings from word parts before checking context."}]}]},{"id":"lab-context-clues","title":"Context Clues: Meanings in the Text","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Context Clue Hunt","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 107–115 (vocabulary words in context)"},{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, find two words from the list in the text (for example *pulverize* on p. 107 and *appraised* on p. 111). Read the sentences around each word. Underline the clue words, then write your own meaning and check it in the vocabulary list."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the sentence around *pulverize* help you figure out its meaning? Is the word positive, negative or neutral?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The sentence is about someone threatening to beat Percy badly, so *pulverize* must mean to crush or totally defeat him. It's a negative, scary word. That shows the character is trying to intimidate him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Appraised* could remind you of *praise*, but is that the meaning here? What clue helps?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"No, it doesn't mean praised. In the sentence, someone looks Percy over carefully, like judging whether he is good enough. So *appraised* means looked at him closely to judge him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Great. The remaining words (*excelled*, *technique*, *fates*, *mortals*, *escort*, *hoard*, *sacrificed*, *demigod*) will appear as we read. When you meet one, stop and use the sentence to check your meaning."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in using context and word parts to determine word meanings and in explaining how word choice affects tone (ELD.PI.6.7, ELD.PI.6.6).","sayAsk":"Say: Show me the clue words in the sentence. Ask: What do the words around *appraised* tell you? Frames: The word ___ means ___ because the sentence says ___. The author chose ___ instead of ___ to show ___. Allow students to say the meaning in their home language first with a partner, then in English.","watchFor":"If students guess a meaning from how the word looks (appraised = praised) → Prompt: 'Read the whole sentence. Does that meaning fit?' If students define a word only with a synonym they cannot explain → Prompt: 'Use it in your own sentence.' Success: students point to clue words and revise their first guess when the text disagrees."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: using context clues","tryThis":"Give students a three-step card: 1) Read the sentence before and after. 2) Circle clue words. 3) Replace the word with your guess and see if it makes sense."},{"type":"situation-placeholder","tryThis":""}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students cite evidence of Percy's changing skills and relationships (RL.6.1). Part B: Students analyze how the sequence of training episodes builds toward capture the flag and the quest (RL.6.5). Part C: Students explain Percy's growth in writing, using the new vocabulary.","activities":[{"id":"lia-cite-training","title":"Part A: Track Percy's Training and Relationships","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3","L.6.6"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 107–116"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 107–116. Make a three-column chart: 1) Training episode (what Percy does), 2) Evidence (a short quote or paraphrase with page number), 3) What it shows about Percy's skill or relationships. Record at least three episodes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A hero-in-training story usually follows a pattern: the hero struggles, gets help from a mentor or friend, tries again, and shows a small success. Each episode is one step in that pattern. As you read, ask: What can Percy do now that he could not do before? Who is he closer to or in conflict with?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Choose one training episode. What is a struggle Percy faces, and what text evidence shows it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On the page where Percy practices (p. ___), the text shows he is behind the other campers and gets frustrated. I know because the narration says he struggles and others notice. That shows he is still a beginner."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Where do you see a success, even a small one? How does that success change how another camper treats him?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When Percy does something well in training, other campers look at him differently. Someone who ignored him before now pays attention, so his relationships are starting to change because he has proved himself a little."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at how Percy talks to Annabeth, Luke or Clarisse in this section. What changes or stays the same?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Annabeth and Luke act like guides who teach him, but Clarisse is still hostile and threatens him. So some relationships are growing closer and one is turning into a rivalry."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3"],"stem":"Which statement best describes how Percy's relationships and skills are changing in pp. 107–116?","choices":[{"text":"Percy quickly masters everything and no longer needs anyone's help.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a believable misunderstanding because heroes in myths are strong, but the text shows Percy struggling and relying on teachers and friends."},{"text":"Percy gains new skills through training while forming closer ties with some campers and facing conflict with others.","correct":true,"rationale":"This matches the evidence: practice and mentors help him improve, while relationships shift in both directions."},{"text":"Percy stays the same because the other campers do not notice his efforts.","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may think a newcomer is ignored, but the text shows campers reacting to him as he trains."},{"text":"Percy's training matters less than the stories about the gods.","correct":false,"rationale":"The myth details are interesting, but the chapter is built around training episodes that shape Percy."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and citing evidence about character change (ELD.PI.6.6) and adding detail to sentences with adverbials (ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner what Percy does, then add *where*, *when* or *how*. Frames: In the training arena, Percy ___. At first, Percy ___, but later he ___. Percy works ___ (carefully/awkwardly/eagerly). Provide a word bank of adverbs and prepositional phrases (in the arena, during the lesson, after practice).","watchFor":"If students retell the whole chapter → Prompt: 'Choose one episode and one piece of evidence.' If sentences are short and bare → Prompt: 'Add a detail about time, place or manner.' Success: students cite a page and expand a sentence with at least one adverbial."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding evidence","tryThis":"Give a page range for each episode (for example, pp. 107–109) and have students look for one sentence that shows Percy's struggle and one that shows a success."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: analyzing relationships","tryThis":"Ask students to compare how two characters treat Percy and explain what each relationship says about the values the camp expects of heroes."}]}]},{"id":"lia-sequence-structure","title":"Part B: How the Sequence Builds Toward Capture the Flag and the Quest","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.1","L.6.4"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 107–116"},{"type":"directions","text":"Use your chart to put the episodes in order on a sequence strip (Episode 1 → Episode 2 → Episode 3 → Capture the Flag / Quest). Under each arrow write what the episode adds that the next one needs. Then think, pair and share."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Authors choose the order of scenes on purpose. When each episode builds on the one before, we can say the structure builds toward something bigger. Here, training scenes prepare readers, and Percy, for capture the flag and for the quest call. Words like *excelled*, *technique* and *fates* help show the shift from practice to destiny."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the first training episode set up that later ones build on?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The first episode shows Percy as a beginner who lacks skill. That sets up the others, because we can see him get better from that starting point."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do the episodes lead toward capture the flag and the quest call? What would be missing if the author skipped the training?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The training shows what skills Percy has and what he still lacks, so when capture the flag comes up, we know he is both ready and at risk. Talk about fates and the quest makes his training feel important, like it has a purpose. If the author skipped it, the quest would feel too sudden."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Words like *fates*, *mortals*, *sacrificed* and *demigod* appear in this section. How do they help show what the camp expects of a hero?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They show that being a demigod is serious. Heroes are not like ordinary mortals, and they might have to give things up, like *sacrificed*. The camp expects heroes to be skilled, brave, loyal and ready for fate."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining how the order of scenes fits the overall structure, using sequence language and evaluating the author's word choices (ELD.PI.6.7, ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Explain the order of events with sequence words. Frames: First, ___. Then ___. Finally, ___. This episode prepares Percy for ___ because ___. The word *fates* makes the chapter feel ___. Let students rehearse with a partner using the sequence strip.","watchFor":"If students list events without explaining how they connect → Prompt: 'What does this episode set up for the next one?' If students use only 'and then' → Prompt: 'Try *as a result* or *because of this*.' Success: students explain at least one cause-and-effect link between episodes."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: structure and sequence","tryThis":"Give students event cards to order, then ask 'What does this event make possible?' for each. Have them complete: This episode matters because it leads to ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: analyzing structure","tryThis":"Ask students to predict how the chapter would feel if the quest call came first and the training second, and to explain why the author chose this order."}]}]},{"id":"lia-quick-write","title":"Part C: Quick Write on Percy's Growth","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.5","L.6.6"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write 4–5 sentences answering: How do Percy's struggles and successes reflect the pattern of a hero in training, and what skills or values does this community expect a hero to develop? Use at least one piece of text evidence with a page number and at least two vocabulary words from today."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Start with a claim, add evidence, then explain. Use sequence words like *first*, *next* and *as a result* to show how the episodes connect."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Sentence starters: In Chapter 8, Percy ___ at first, but later ___ (p. __). This episode leads to ___. The camp expects heroes to ___. For example, the text says ___, which shows ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 8, Percy struggles at first with training, but he slowly improves with help from Luke and Annabeth (p. 110). Each episode prepares him for capture the flag and for the quest. The camp expects heroes to practice their technique, be loyal and be ready to face their fates. For example, the talk about being a demigod and about what heroes sacrificed shows that heroes must be brave and give things up."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Listen for: a claim about change, a cited detail, and an explanation linking an episode to what comes next. Collect these as a formative check on RL.6.1 and RL.6.5 and use them to plan flex time."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing evidence-based sentences with precise vocabulary and added detail (ELD.PI.6.7, ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Rehearse your first sentence aloud, then write it. Frames: At first, Percy ___; later, he ___ because ___. The camp expects heroes to ___ and ___. Provide a word bank with the ten vocabulary words and several adverbials.","watchFor":"If students write opinions ('I like Percy') → Prompt: 'Tell what the text shows, not how you feel.' If evidence has no explanation → Prompt: 'Add a sentence that begins with *This shows*.' Success: students use two vocabulary words accurately and link evidence to a claim."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: writing the paragraph","tryThis":"Provide a three-sentence frame (claim, evidence, explanation) and let students say the sentences to a partner before writing. Allow speech-to-text."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: writing","tryThis":"Ask students to add a sentence about how a myth pattern of a hero in training appears in this chapter, using *although* or *as a result* to connect ideas."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students consolidate how a sequence of events shows character growth and reflect on vocabulary learned.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-reflection","title":"Reflection: Sequence Shows Growth","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.3","RL.6.5","L.6.6"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In your Performance Task, you will describe how a sequence of events shows a character growing. Today you practiced exactly that with Percy."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete: The sequence of training episodes in Chapter 8 shows that Percy ___. One word from today that helped me explain this is ___ because ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The sequence of training episodes in Chapter 8 shows that Percy is changing from a beginner into someone camp leaders think is ready for bigger challenges. One word from today that helped me explain this is *technique* because it names the skill he is learning, and improving it shows his growth."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (optional)","purpose":"Students continue reading and begin a cross-cultural hero text.","activities":[{"id":"homework-reading","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1) Read and annotate The Lightning Thief, Chapter 8 (pp. 117–126). Mark one place where Percy's skills or relationships change. 2) Read and annotate the excerpt from the Popol Vuh. Mark one detail about the heroes' trials that reminds you of Percy's training."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students reread Chapter 8 (pp. 107–116) to cite Percy's training episodes and his changing relationships, and analyze how the order of those episodes builds toward capture the flag and the quest call. They also decode and use ten vocabulary words through syllabication and context clues.","keyActivities":["Turn and Talk about struggle and success in learning","Syllabication and context clue practice with Chapter 8 vocabulary","Three-column evidence chart of Percy's training episodes and relationships","Sequence strip and Think-Pair-Share on structure building toward capture the flag and the quest","Quick Write on Percy's growth and the values expected of heroes"],"vocabularyTaught":["pulverize","excelled","technique","appraised","fates","mortals","escort","hoard","sacrificed","demigod"],"standardsCovered":["RL.6.1","RL.6.5","L.6.4","L.6.6","RL.6.3","RL.6.10"]}}
